_help: Daily Artifact Guesser bank. Entries rotate in this order, one per day, starting 2026-11-20 (see FIRST_DAY in daily-artifact-core.mjs). point = [lon, lat] of where it was made or found; year is negative for BCE and is the single number that is scored (dateLabel is what students read). Give sketchfab (a Sketchfab model id), image (a site-relative path) or both. clue must not name the artifact or its place. Reuse images and models a lesson already credits.

credit3d.text: OTZI, THE ICEMAN. PREHISTORIC MAN SCAN by jesusmolina on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Ötzi the Iceman
artifacts.place: Ötztal Alps, on the Italy–Austria border
artifacts.clue: Hikers spotted him in 1991, sticking out of melting ice high in the mountains. He had been waiting there for thousands of years.
artifacts.blurb: A man killed around 5,300 years ago and frozen where he fell. His copper axe, flint knife, bow and stuffed leather shoes are a snapshot of life at the hinge between the Stone and Bronze Ages.

artifacts.name: Cyrus Cylinder
artifacts.clue: A clay barrel covered in wedge-shaped writing. Its text says a conquering king was welcomed into a great city and let captive peoples go home.
artifacts.blurb: Written in Babylonian cuneiform after Cyrus of Persia took Babylon in 539 BCE. It fits the biblical story of exiles returning home, though it never names Judah.

credit3d.text: 1903 Wright Flyer by byrikardo3D on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: 1903 Wright Flyer
artifacts.clue: It flew for twelve seconds on a windy beach and changed the century. Its builders ran a bicycle shop.
artifacts.blurb: The first powered, controlled, heavier-than-air flight. Wilbur and Orville Wright tested wing shapes in their own wind tunnel before they ever left the ground.

credit2d.text: Photo: M. Strasser via Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 2.0

artifacts.name: Pectoral of Tutankhamun
artifacts.place: Tomb KV62, Valley of the Kings, Egypt
artifacts.clue: Gold, lapis lazuli and a winged beetle. The beetle’s name is one piece of the owner’s own name. The tomb was found nearly untouched in 1922.
artifacts.blurb: A winged scarab (ḫpr) sits under a cartouche for the throne name Nebkheperure. The jewel repeats the king’s name as a picture.

credit3d.text: Stonehenge England – VR by GSXNet on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Stonehenge
artifacts.clue: Giant standing stones in a circle on open grassland frame the sunrise on the longest day of the year.
artifacts.blurb: Built in stages over centuries by people with no metal tools. Some of its smaller bluestones were hauled about 240 km from Wales.

artifacts.name: The Gutenberg Bible
artifacts.clue: The first major book printed from movable metal type. About 180 copies were made, and artists added the colored capital letters by hand.
artifacts.blurb: Johannes Gutenberg’s 42-line Latin Bible. Cheap, fast copying pushed the Reformation, the Scientific Revolution and mass literacy.

credit3d.text: The Great Pyramid of Giza by ianicolo on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
artifacts.clue: For almost 4,000 years this was the tallest structure humans had ever built. Millions of limestone blocks, one great river nearby.
artifacts.blurb: Built for the pharaoh Khufu in the Fourth Dynasty. Surveying, quarrying and feeding tens of thousands of workers was as impressive as the stone.

artifacts.name: The Tel Dan Stele
artifacts.clue: Broken pieces of a victory monument, found reused in a wall. A rival king’s Aramaic inscription seems to mention a “house of David.”
artifacts.blurb: The earliest widely accepted reference outside the Bible to David’s dynasty, written by an enemy about 150 years after David.

credit3d.text: Apollo 11 Command Module by Smithsonian Institution on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Apollo 11 Command Module Columbia
artifacts.place: Kennedy Space Center, Florida, USA (launch site)
artifacts.clue: A cone-shaped capsule that carried three people around the Moon and back, then splashed down in an ocean.
artifacts.blurb: Columbia was the only part of the giant Saturn V that came home. Armstrong and Aldrin landed in the lunar module while Michael Collins stayed in orbit with this capsule.

credit2d.text: Schøyen Collection photograph via Wikimedia Commons · Commons marks public domain; CDLI credits © Martin Schøyen and the Schøyen Collection

artifacts.name: Adab administrative tablet
artifacts.clue: Ruled boxes and wedge-shaped marks: an accountant’s record from the days when writing was still young.
artifacts.blurb: An early Sumerian account from the city of Adab. Much of the oldest writing in the world was not poetry or law but bookkeeping.

credit3d.text: Armenian Khachkar Stone Memorial by University of South Florida Libraries on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Amenaprkich Khachkar
artifacts.clue: A cross carved into stone as fine as lace, from a mountain monastery in a land that made Christianity its state religion in 301.
artifacts.blurb: A khachkar (“cross-stone”) is a memorial found only in Armenian Christian culture. This one, “the Savior,” has stood through seven centuries of weather.

artifacts.name: The Pilate Stone (replica)
artifacts.clue: A Latin dedication that names the Roman governor who ordered a famous trial. The original was later reused as a building block in a theater.
artifacts.blurb: Rare physical evidence outside the Gospels for Pontius Pilate, prefect of Judea. The one pictured is a replica; the original is in the Israel Museum.

credit3d.text: Göbekli Tepe by mbarngrover on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Göbekli Tepe
artifacts.clue: Hunter-gatherers carved T-shaped pillars with foxes, snakes and boars on a hilltop. This was before farming, pottery or metal.
artifacts.blurb: The oldest known temple complex. It turned the old story upside down: monuments may have come before farming, not after.

credit2d.text: Ardon Bar Hama / Israel Museum · Public domain

artifacts.name: The Great Isaiah Scroll
artifacts.clue: A scroll about seven meters long, sealed in a clay jar in a desert cave. It is a thousand years older than the next oldest complete copy of its text.
artifacts.blurb: Found in 1947 among the Dead Sea Scrolls. It matches the later Hebrew text astonishingly closely, which shows how carefully scribes copied.

credit3d.text: The world's first Printing Press by Michael Mirn on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Gutenberg’s printing press
artifacts.clue: A goldsmith in a Rhine River city bent the idea of a wine press to squeeze ink onto paper from tiny metal letters.
artifacts.blurb: Movable type made books cheap and fast to copy, and every big idea after it traveled faster.

credit2d.text: Photo: Shonagon via Wikimedia Commons · CC0

artifacts.name: Stela of Minnakht
artifacts.clue: A scribe ordered this limestone slab for his tomb. Two jackals and two protective eyes mirror each other across the top.
artifacts.blurb: Made for Minnakht, chief of the scribes, in the reign of Pharaoh Ay. The Louvre records it as coming from Akhmim.

credit3d.text: The Creation of Adam by Loïc Norgeot on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: The Creation of Adam
artifacts.clue: Two nearly touching fingers, painted on a ceiling over four years by an artist who called himself a sculptor, not a painter.
artifacts.blurb: Michelangelo’s fresco, commissioned by Pope Julius II. It fuses Christian story with Renaissance study of the human body.

credit2d.text: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

artifacts.name: Jehoiachin ration tablet
artifacts.clue: A palace clerk listed oil rations for exiled royalty in a captured capital. A king from a conquered kingdom appears by name.
artifacts.blurb: A Babylonian ration list that names Jehoiachin of Judah. It independently confirms a king the Bible says was exiled to Babylon.

credit3d.text: Lascaux by Geoffrey Marchal on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Lascaux Cave
artifacts.clue: Walls painted by flickering lamplight with bulls, horses and deer, found in 1940 by four teenagers and a dog.
artifacts.blurb: Hundreds of paintings made by people who studied animals closely long before anyone farmed them.

artifacts.name: The Erastus Inscription
artifacts.clue: A line of Latin carved in a paving stone says an official paid for the pavement out of his own pocket. Paul greets an official with this name.
artifacts.blurb: ERASTVS PRO AEDILITATE SVA PECVNIA STRAVIT. It matches “Erastus, the city treasurer” in Romans 16:23.

credit3d.text: The Royal Game Of Ur by Greektoys.org on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: The Royal Game of Ur
artifacts.clue: A racing board game buried with its owner in a royal grave. Its rules were decoded from a clay tablet written long afterward.
artifacts.blurb: The oldest known board game. Students today can still play it from the reconstructed rules.

credit2d.text: Papyrus 115 (P.Oxy. LXVI 4499), Sackler Library, Oxford · Public domain

artifacts.name: Papyrus 115
artifacts.clue: A scrap of Greek on papyrus, saved by dry desert sand. It gives a famous number as 616, not the more familiar 666.
artifacts.blurb: Found at Oxyrhynchus, one of the oldest copies of Revelation 13. Early Christians copied, compared and argued about the text.

credit3d.text: The Rosetta Stone by The British Museum on Sketchfab

credit2d.text: Photo: Hans Hillewaert via Wikimedia Commons · CC BY-SA 4.0

artifacts.name: The Rosetta Stone
artifacts.clue: One slab of dark stone, three kinds of writing. Comparing them let scholars read a language nobody had read for 1,400 years.
artifacts.blurb: A priestly decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic and Greek, found in 1799 by soldiers rebuilding a fort. Champollion used it to crack Egyptian writing in 1822.

credit2d.text: Stele of Hammurabi · Louvre Museum Sb 8 · Public domain

artifacts.name: Code of Hammurabi
artifacts.place: Babylon, Iraq (carried to Susa, Iran, as war loot)
artifacts.clue: 282 laws carved into black stone, with a king shown receiving them from a god at the top. “An eye for an eye” is one of them.
artifacts.blurb: Law moved from a ruler’s whim to public, written rules anyone could read. It was made in Babylon, but taken to Susa centuries later, which is where it was dug up in 1901.

credit3d.text: Sumerian Axe by Milacetious on Sketchfab

artifacts.name: Sumerian Axe
artifacts.clue: Cast in the land between two rivers, where cities, writing and the wheel were all new ideas.
artifacts.blurb: The Sumerians worked copper and bronze alongside writing, law and long-distance trade.

credit2d.text: Photographed by the British Museum via Wikimedia Commons · Public domain

artifacts.name: Book of the Dead of Ani
artifacts.clue: A heart is weighed against a feather. Fail the test and a monster eats it. This was painted on papyrus to help the dead pass.
artifacts.blurb: The Weighing of the Heart from the Book of the Dead made for the scribe Ani. Thoth, god of writing, records the verdict.
